segments.text: So far we have been working with variables that can hold one piece of data, like floats, integers, strings, and booleans.

code_cells.content:
x=15.5 # float
y=10 # integer
z="Hello There" # string
w=True #Boolean
print(x,y,z,w)

segments.text: There are also objects in Python that can hold multiple items of data. These include lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets. This week we will talk about lists.
As you might imagine, a list is an object that can hold a list of items.
A list is a kind of sequence object in Python because the items in the list have an order.

items: You create a list in Python using bracket notation.
The code below will create a list in Python that holds three integers-- 1, 2, and 3-- in that order
You can think of a list as a "book" that holds a series of sheets of paper, each of holds one item.
You can print lists.

segments.text: Lists can be composed of a single data type or a mix of data types.
You can use the repetition operator ("*") to have Python repeat a list, much as we have done with strings.
You can use the concatenation ("+") to combine lists, much as we have done with strings.

code_cells.content:
my_list=[1,2,3]
print(my_list)

l1=["Adam","Eve","Cain","Abel"]
l2=["Joe",True,4.1,5]
print(l1)
print(l2)

# this will create a list consisting of 12 strings.
song=["Tra","La","La"]*4
print(song)

# here a line of a song is represented by a list of the words in that line.
line1=["Ob", "la", "di"]
line2=["Ob", "la", "da"]
combinedLines=line1+line2
print(combinedLines)

items: You can index into lists in a similar manner that you did with strings. In the case of strings, indeces pull out individual characters; in the case of lists they pull out individual list elements.
The first index into a list is zero.

code_cells.content:
line1=["Ob", "la", "di"]
line2=["Ob", "la", "da"]
combinedLines=line1+line2

print(combinedLines)
print(combinedLines[0])
print(combinedLines[2])
print(combinedLines[-1])

segments.text: Lists, unlike strings, are mutable. That means that their elements can be changed.

code_cells.content:
# create a list
l=[1,2,3]
print(l)
# change its third element
l[2]=99
print(l)

items: List variables are "references"
That means that they point to objects in memory, and more than one variable can point to the same object. The following creates one list and then sets it up so that two variables point to that list.

segments.text: This means that if you change the list using one of the variables, the change will be reflected in the other one as well.

code_cells.content:
mylist=[1,2,3]
mylist2=mylist
print(mylist)
print(mylist2)

mylist=[1,2,3]
mylist2=mylist
mylist2[0]=999
print(mylist)
print(mylist2)

items: Python will only create new lists when you use the square bracket list creation syntax
You can take advantage of this behavior to create true copies of your list objects, as in the following example:

code_cells.content:
mylist1=[1,2,3] # this creates a list object
mylist2=[]+mylist1 # this creates a second, distinct list object (with the same structure as the first)
mylist1[0]=999 # therefore this only changes the first object
print(mylist1)
print(mylist2)

segments.text: Either of the following creates an empty list with no elements in it.
Sometimes you want to create a list with a certain number of identical elements. You can do this with the "*" operator. The following creates a list of 10 zeros.

code_cells.content:
mylist1=[]
mylist2=list()
print(mylist1)
print(mylist2)

mylist=[0]*10
print(mylist)

lecture_blocks.title: Creating Lists Using the Range Function

segments.text: You can also create lists using the range function. For instance, if you want the multiples of 5 between 5 and 100, do the following:

code_cells.content:
m5=list(range(5,101,5))
print(m5)

lecture_blocks.title: Looping Over the Values of a List

segments.text: You can loop over the values of a list using the "in" keyword, as in the following. Each time through, your loop variable takes on the next value in the list.

lecture_blocks.title: Drawbacks to Using "for" Loops with "in" to iterate through a list

items: A "for" loop is a convenient way to iterate through a list
The loop target variable assumes the value of each list item in turn
However, you can't change the list this way. See the following example:

code_cells.content:
mylist=[1,2,3]
for n in mylist:
  n=n*5
# no effect on the list!
print(mylist)

items: In order to change a list item, you need to know the index of the item you wish to change. For example:

code_cells.content:
mylist=[1,2,3]
mylist[1]=444
print(mylist)

lecture_blocks.title: Iterating Over a List Using Index Values

segments.text: There are two techniques for iterating over a list using index values. They are:

items: Setting up a counter variable outside the loop and continually updating the variable as you move to the next position in the list
Using the range() function to create a custom range that represents the size of your list

segments.text: You can add a counter variable to your "for" loop to keep track of the list index. The following code doubles each element in the list.

code_cells.content:
mylist=[1,2,3]
counter=0
for _ in mylist:
  mylist[counter]*=2
  counter+=1
print(mylist)

segments.text: The range function will also generate all of the indeces of the list, when combined with the len function. The following code is another way to double all of the elements of a list.

code_cells.content:
mylist=[1,2,3]
for i in range(len(mylist)):
  mylist[i]*=2
print(mylist)

items: You can extract multiple items from a list.
This is done with slicing; the syntax for this is the same as what we saw for strings.
As was the case with strings, the slicing syntax is similar to the range function

code_cells.content:
names=["Amy","Bob","Carol","Dave","Eddie","Flo"]
someNames=names[1:4]
print(someNames)

moreNames=names[-2:]
print(moreNames)

otherNames=names[0:-1:2]
print(otherNames)

The index method gives the index of an item in a list. If the item is not in the list, it gives an error.

items:
You have already seen a couple of ways in which you can add items to a list:

Repeat the list with the "*" operator

Concatenate two lists together with the "+" operator
Another way is to use the append method. It allows you to add an item to the end of a list.

code_cells.content:

print(mylist)

You can use the sort method to sort a list (numerically or alphabetically). It replaces the list with the sorted version.

code_cells.content:
fruits=['melon','orange','banana']
fruits.append('apple')
print(fruits)
fruits.sort()
print(fruits)
sequence=list(range(10,0,-1))
print(sequence)
sequence.sort()
print(sequence)

You can use the max and min functions to find the largest and smallest elements of a list.

code_cells.content:
prices = [3.99, 2.99, 1.99]
print(f"The highest price is ${max(prices)} and the lowest price is ${min(prices)}.")

segments.text: You can use the "remove" method to remove an item from the list.
It will generate an error if it is not in the list, so you might want to check if it is using the "in" operator first.

code_cells.content:
prices=[3.99,2.99,1.99]
prices.remove(2.99)
print(prices)

lecture_blocks.title: Removing an Item by its Position

segments.text: You can also use the "del" keyword to remove an item by specifying its index position.

code_cells.content:
prices=[3.99,2.99,1.99]
del prices[1]
print(prices)

segments.text: You can use the "reverse" method on list to reverse the order of its elements.
This will not sort the list, but will just reverse the order.

code_cells.content:
names=["Alan","Betty","Dave","Chris"]
names.reverse()
print(names)
